chapter: Los Angeles scene and the Ellington sound
title: On a Turquoise Cloud and Kay Davis's metal derby
summary: Brown shows how the singer's piercing voice was muted with a towel in a derby on the record.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: In Stanley Dance's book, The World of Duke Ellington, he quotes you as saying that you decided to write your own showcase for trombone. One was the Golden Crest and then you mentioned also that you wrote On a Turquoise Cloud.
Yes.
And I see that On a Turquoise Cloud you have co-composer credit. Your name, right ahead of Ellington's.
Uh-huh.

And we just played that record, which according to the Asland disography was recorded December 22nd, 1947, and in hearing the record it reminded you of something rather unusual in the recording, right?
You mean the vocal?
Yes.
Ah, yes, this young lady that was vocalist with us, Kay Davis, was a graduate of Northwestern University in the field of music, and her voice was very, very

beautiful, very, very piercing, very, very -- well, whatever. And this number that we recorded, she was part of an instrumental trio, and her voice pierced through everything so strong that we had to find some way to shade her voice down without destroying her delivery.

So I finally rigged up the outfit of taking a metal derby, which we use in orchestra work, and putting a cloth towel inside the metal derby, and letting her sing with this in front -- right directly in front of her mouth, so that when you hear this record it sounds like she is open like the rest of the horns, but actually she is singing into a metal derby with a towel inside it.
How close was the metal derby to her face?
Actually, she couldn't see anything past the metal derby. It was right in her face.
A couple of inches away.
Yeah.
And where was the microphone?
Well, the mike was --
She had one of her own?
No, she didn't. They sang to a common mike, you know, it was sitting out by itself. But that's the only way we could get her voice toned down so that it would fit with the rest of these instruments.
Where was -- do you remember where that was recorded?
I think that was New York. I think it was -- it isn't -- wasn't on the record saying where it was recorded, huh?
I don't believe so.
Okay, well anyway, that's the way it was recorded.
